articles.title: What telecoms leave behind when they exit a country
articles.author: Ranking Digital Rights
paras: When telecoms pull out of markets, data protection and human rights commitments often disappear
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Akil Mazumder via Pexels. Used under a Pexels license.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In March 2022, just over a year after Myanmar’s military coup, Telenor, the Norwegian telecommunications giant, sold its subsidiary in the country to M1 Group, bringing nearly eight years of operation to an end. But leaving Myanmar did not end the controversy surrounding its departure. Instead, the hasty exit came back to haunt the company over the next four years.

Since then, criticisms, lawsuits and litigation by civil society and affected people have continued to follow the company. The scrutiny also reached a crescendo this September, when Norwegian authorities opened criminal investigations into Telenor over allegations of aiding crimes against humanity in the country and transferring sanctioned surveillance equipment during the sale. Within days, a court in Norway also green-lit a class-action lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Telenor’s former customers in Myanmar.

Telenor reiterated its position upon the investigation, arguing that any alternatives would have endangered the employees’ lives. Yet the company’s trouble raises a broader question that many telecommunication multinationals may have to confront one day: When a company decides to exit a “high-risk market,” where does its responsibility end?
Leaving is not just a business decision

Under military rule, Telenor faced government demands to facilitate surveillance, hand over the personal data of dissidents and activists, and restrict access to information. In a market like this, staying may cease to be viable. For a telecom operator, the matter is not simply to make a choice between remaining in the market or leaving, but whether it can exit in a way that minimizes further harm to users, without leaving them more vulnerable. Unfortunately, Telenor failed to do so.

In a conventional asset sale involving multinational companies, the transaction may center largely around physical and commercial assets, such as factories, equipment, and inventory. Selling a telecom subsidiary is another story. As gatekeepers of internet access and digital information, telcos control sensitive user data, including location records and device logs. They also serve as key intermediaries for interception systems and have the technical capacity to cut off network access. In a sale, the company hands over not just infrastructure and commercial assets, but also systems and data that can expose the movements and footprints of millions of users.

Without rigorous buyer scrutiny and assessments of the risks associated with the transfer, a corporate sale may lead to grave harm to users, who might be watched, tracked, or even silenced in authoritarian contexts.

What followed in Myanmar showed that the risk was anything but hypothetical. It also revealed why powerful companies cannot simply shed their responsibilities by selling their business, when people depending on their services are left to bear the consequences.
A global pull back is underway

This matters because Telenor’s withdrawal from Myanmar is hardly an isolated case. After the debacle, the telecom giant began systematically pulling back from its Asian markets. In 2022, the company combined its Malaysian subsidiary Digi with local telecom service Celcom. In Thailand the following year, it merged its local business dtac with True Corporation before later selling down most of its stake in the entity. It also completed its sale of Telenor Pakistan to PTCL at the end of 2025, with further plans to dispense with its remaining Asian assets.

Zooming out, multinational telecom operators are shrinking the overseas footprints they spent decades building. MTN, Africa’s largest telecom operator, announced its plan to “orderly exit” from the Middle East in 2020 amid geopolitical risks. The company has ended its operations in Syria, Yemen, and Afghanistan by 2025. MTN also completed the sale of its operations in Guinea-Bissau and Guinea-Conakry in 2024, citing unsustainable costs.

Aiming to refocus on a small group of more profitable core markets — Britain, Brazil, Germany, and Spain — Spanish telecom giant Telefónica also accelerated its retreat from Spanish-speaking Latin America. In 2025 alone, it sold its subsidiaries in Argentina, Peru, Uruguay, and Ecuador, followed by exits from Colombia, Chile, and Mexico in early 2026.

The reasons for telecoms’ departure vary from geopolitical tensions to high costs. However, we should ask the critical question: what changes for the customers after a telecom operator leaves them behind?
What gets lost in the handover

While the network will continue to provide service to users, the transparency practices and internal procedures and protocols for data safeguards may change after a sale. This is where the risks of market exit are less visible. Telenor, MTN, and Telefónica have all developed sophisticated governance systems, including formal human rights policies, data-protection and security procedures, and regular transparency reporting. Research shows they are among the strongest performers on transparency and accountability in the telecom industry.

Those transparency reports provide a useful window into how telcos handle government demands. The reports describe the procedures in place to respond to government requests for user data, content restrictions, and network disruptions, and publish data on such requests across different markets. Although transparency alone cannot prevent abuse, it creates a public record of how governments exert pressure on companies.

However, we found that transparency reporting mostly does not survive ownership changes. Once a multinational operator leaves a market, it naturally stops reporting in that country. Disappointingly, its successors overwhelmingly fail to maintain the same level of transparency.

Millicom, a recurring buyer of Telefónica’s Latin American assets, acquired its operations in Uruguay and Ecuador, and a controlling stake in Colombia. Millicom does publish law-enforcement disclosures, but the data are aggregated by region rather than by country. Moreover, as of September 2026, only the 2024 report is publicly available. Elsewhere, the picture is even bleaker: None of the other recent buyers appeared to publish transparency reports or commit to continuing their predecessors’ transparency practices.

The discontinuation of transparency reporting removes the opportunity for the public to scrutinize whether or not the volume of the government demands changed after each ownership transition. It also hides from view how those demands are handled internally.

Transparency reporting, however, is only the tip of the iceberg. Beneath it lies a much broader mechanism of user data protections, institutional norms, and governance safeguards, such as risk escalation channels, legal and human rights checks, and many more.

In authoritarian states, multinational telcos are no less likely to face government pressure to shut down networks, block websites, or hand over user data. While these companies may also have limited room to resist, they usually operate under more institutional oversight than state-controlled ones. They are also exposed to more scrutiny from the international press and civil society, greater reputational risk, and often stronger regulatory frameworks established by their home countries.

By contrast, many operators who succeeded these businesses might be more closely connected to governments and more deeply embedded in the local political and regulatory environment. Facing fewer external constraints from society, media, and NGOs, they also have less willingness and fewer resources to challenge governments.
What a more responsible exit might look like

Since safeguards may weaken or even disappear with ownership shift, the essential duty to protect users’ rights should not be treated as an afterthought to a market exit. It must be a key element of the transaction.

For telecom companies, a responsible exit should begin well before a buyer is even selected. Before entering Myanmar in 2014, Telenor commissioned a human rights impact assessment (HRIA) for its planned market entry. The company also states that it considered human rights and data privacy as it prepared for its departure. But there is no public record showing that Telenor conducted a standalone assessment of the human rights risks of the exit itself.

Companies should commission a mandated, exit-specific human rights impact assessment, evaluating what user risks the sale itself might create, the concerns of stakeholders and users, how the data might be used or transferred in the future, and which groups of users would be most exposed to the risks it identifies.

Buyer due diligence should go beyond financial stability to examine the buyer’s human rights record, its capacity to govern sensitive data, and whether existing safeguards can survive under new ownership.

Moreover, a responsible exit from any politically risky market should also ask a basic question: What should not be transferred in a sale? Should every piece of user data be handed over to the next owner? Telecom companies should evaluate if any sensitive data can be segregated, anonymized, or even deleted whenever feasible, particularly when transferring such data could expose high-risk users.

Similarly, some technical infrastructure, such as surveillance equipment, interception systems, and other network-control capabilities, should not be bundled into a sale automatically as ordinary infrastructure. Norwegian authorities are now probing whether Telenor transferred sanctioned surveillance equipment as part of the sale of Telenor Myanmar without the required authorization from the Norwegian government.
A new test for the next exit

If Telenor offers a lesson for everyone about what can go wrong in a reckless departure from a high-risk market, MTN’s unfinished exit from Iran may offer a test about whether companies can approach their next departure differently.

MTN still holds a 49 percent stake in Irancell. The current U.S. sanctions on Iran also complicate any attempt to exit. Earlier this year, MTN also protested after the CEO of Irancell was ousted by the Iranian authorities over delaying an internet blackout order during the domestic protest. This arguably makes MTN’s position in Iran even more difficult than Telenor’s trajectory in Myanmar. When MTN is finally able to withdraw from the country, can it exit in a more responsible way?

articles.title: How K-dramas use Africa as a backdrop to boost South Korea’s image
articles.author: Osarugue Otebele, Assistant Professor, Cinema Studies Institute, University of Toronto
paras: The success of South Korean popular music or K-pop continues to power the Hallyu Wave, a term that describes the global obsession with the country’s pop culture production.

But before K-pop came the spread of K-drama, TV series from the country, starting in the late 1990s. By 2024 the melodrama Queen of Tears ranked as the most watched Korean series on Netflix, becoming the 14th most watched show of all time on the streaming service. It followed on the success of many other hits like Crash Landing on You and Marry My Husband.
K-drama has led to the development of another trend: Africa repeatedly appears as a homogeneous place full of savage danger or childish immaturity, and in need of a Korean saviour.

As a scholar of film and media, with a specific interest in global Black art and film practices, I recently studied how and why Africa became this trope in K-drama. This is particularly true in rags-to-riches romance stories and melodramas.
I traced Africa’s presence in three K-dramas – Shooting Stars (2022), Marry My Husband (2024) and Queen of Tears (2024). In them, Africa appears in three different negative ways:
a place of rebellion and savagery
a place of punishment for a “troubled” child.

My intention wasn’t to say why these portrayals are bad, but rather to understand what they reveal about South Korea. How they function as a scale for measuring and emphasising South Korea’s own development.
No longer the poor post-war country of the late 1950s, South Korea can now position itself among leading world powers. It has grown in the global economic and cultural landscapes.

Yet, as I argue in my study, what allows countries like this to define their developmental status is their ability to distinguish themselves from Africa. I propose that Africa’s presence in K-dramas is as a place maker, or specifically image-maker. Africa’s “savage” presence serves as a way of distinguishing the emerging soft power of South Korea, where what benefits the country’s global image is the ability to provide aid to Africa.

In his book On the Postcolony, Cameroonian philosopher Achille Mbembe describes Africa as Europe’s “signifier”. This means that the way Europe comes to know and define itself is only possible through how it defines itself against Africa.

But my study contributes to showing that this is not just the case in the west. The ever-growing presence of eastern soft powers such as China and South Korea means that longstanding stereotypes of Africa have found new sites of replenishment.

There are some major threads that connected Africa’s presence in the K-dramas I studied. One is its portrayal as a place where non-Africans could go to build character by participating in volunteer work as part of an NGO. In Marry my Husband, for example, the show’s antagonist Oh Yu-ra loses her job in the family business and is sent to “join a volunteer foundation in Africa to build character”.

In Shooting Stars, this idea of Africa as the epicentre of charity is even more apparent. The show’s opening sequence features the main character digging wells in Africa. He’s accompanied by smiling village children and a sound that one viewer described as “Lion King music”.

In both shows, South Korea is personified through the characters sent to Africa. While Yu-ra is sent as punishment, the character in Shooting Stars is an actor whose volunteer trip aids in his public image in South Korea. Africa becomes what builds the image and character of others, but only by being relegated to a cliché.

Yu-ra’s punishment shows how Africa becomes the K-drama’s vessel to hold the unwanted or defamed of other nations. It collects what disrupts the happiness of romance and, by extension, of nation-making, in South Korea. This figuration of the continent reappears in Queen of Tears.

Queen of Tears does not follow the Asian-saviour-in-Africa trope. Instead, it presents Africa as a place for youthful inhibitions, with no sense of order or rule of law. The ideal place for the kinds of behaviours that might be illegal in the more “civilized” South Korean society that the character exists in.
In Africa’s brief cameo in the show’s third episode, the younger brother of the show’s protagonist, Soo-Cheol, reminisces on his rebellious days:
I’m reminded of when I went to Africa. My twenties were filled with wildness and barbarism.
When chided that he stayed in his hotel for most of the trip, Soo-Cheol comments, “I had enough of the wildness just looking out of the window.”

Here, Africa is understood in proximity to danger and savagery. Is it that there are no crime, criminals, or places and people in need of saving in South Korea? The obvious answer is no, but as my study finds, when viewed through these shows, the answer reads more like, “Compared to Africa, yes.”
Where will Africa go next?

This treatment of Africa began long before the shows in my study. Africa’s character-building qualities appear, for example, in the 2018 film Burning. The film’s female protagonist goes on a “soul-searching” quest to find life’s greater meaning.
In unscripted variety shows, African immigrants living in South Korea, like Sam Okyere or Jonathan Yiombi, often feature as hosts or guests, but not without their share of racist backlash.

Okyere, for example, was subject to racist comments after criticising a video of South Korean students recreating a popular video from his home country, Ghana. The same happened to Yiombi after South Korea was eliminated from the football World Cup because the DRC, his country of birth, defeated Uzbekistan, indirectly causing South Korea to be eliminated.

For better or worse, Africa’s metaphorical and literal presence has come to occupy South Korea’s cultural and aesthetic imagination. Despite Africa also being a continent full of modern urban life, cultural riches and innovation, the clichés remain.

This presence is only possible through the expected and invented image of the savage, helpless and primitive, who is in need, even after independence, of more civilising. And not only from western colonial powers, but also from the growing economies of the east.
K-dramas are increasingly popular in Africa, yet when constantly viewed this way, Hallyu’s success in Africa comes with a heavy representational price.

Despite their engagement with K-drama, African audiences can only ever seem to see themselves represented through a colonial gaze that benefits South Korea’s pursuit of global power. Africa then, while continuing to build South Korea’s cultural capital, can only ever exist as a symbol of lack.

articles.title: America’s death penalty: why executions are rising again
articles.author: Grace Jennings-Edquist, Executive Producer, Podcasts, The Conversation
paras: After two decades of decline, the number of executions in the United States began rising sharply again in 2025. Last year, 47 people were put to death – the highest number in more than 15 years. So far in 2026, another 31 people have been executed.

The resurgence comes amid renewed controversy over capital punishment, following the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee and a proposal to livestream a military execution, which President Donald Trump subsequently walked back.
But according to Carolyn Strange, emeritus professor of history at the Australian National University, these controversies have striking precedents in American history.
Pike is not the first person to survive an execution attempt. In 1946, Willie Francis survived the electric chair in Louisiana. After an unsuccessful legal challenge, the state executed him in 1947.

Strange says the history of capital punishment in the US is marked by repeated attempts to make executions more humane – or at least appear that way. From the electric chair to lethal injections, new methods were introduced with the promise of making death quicker and more efficient.
Lethal injection, for example, has the appearance of an ordinary medical procedure. “It seems normal, it seems clean, it seems clinical, civilised,” Strange says.
Yet Pike’s case raises questions about whether the method has lived up to that promise.
Strange also argues it’s misleading to talk about a single American approach to the death penalty.
It’s really better to talk about the death penalty in the disunited states.

While some states abolished capital punishment more than a century ago, others continue to embrace it. Florida, under governor Ron DeSantis, has been responsible for a substantial share of the recent rise in executions. In 2025, Florida carried out 19 executions – 40% of the year’s total.

And while support in the US for the death penalty has declined over recent decades, the issue remains deeply divisive. For Strange, the history of capital punishment reveals something fundamental about American politics:
The most important thing is that capital punishment and the death penalty is about politics, not justice.

articles.title: Youth protests across Europe: the overlapping crises facing Gen Z
articles.author: Alina Cosma, Assistant Professor of Psychology, Trinity College Dublin
paras: Young people are facing a future that feels increasingly uncertain. Although every generation experiences turbulence while navigating adolescence, the pressures experienced by Gen Z – those born between 1997 and 2012 – are different and seem more pervasive.

From climate change and mental health concerns to academic pressure, housing costs, job and economic insecurity, today’s young people are navigating a complex set of expectations. Understanding their frustrations, including those expressed through protests across Europe, requires looking beyond individual experiences to the social conditions shaping their lives.

Adolescence has long been seen as a period of “storm and stress”. This reflecting a belief that is a universal and inevitable period of emotional turmoil, behavioural conflict and identity crisis. However, this has been increasingly challenged.

Rather than being defined solely by difficulty and disruption, adolescence is increasingly viewed as a period of possibility, opportunity and growth. Yet realising that potential depends heavily on the social environments in which young people grow up.

A growing body of evidence highlights adolescence as a critical developmental period with profound implications for future health and wellbeing. There is also increasing recognition that adolescence extends well beyond the teenage years and well into the twenties.
Young people nowadays grow up under intense and often overlapping pressure, and today this is to a higher extent than generations before.
Evidence from the World Health Organization’s Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study suggests that school-related pressure increased between 2002 and 2022 across many countries.

In 2022, among 15-year-old girls, almost two-thirds reported feeling pressured by schoolwork, compared with less than half of boys. The same research documented declines in perceived family and peer support. In other words, young people appear to be facing increasing demands while some of the social resources that help them cope with those demands are weakening.

Parental expectations and criticism have also intensified in many contexts. Success is increasingly framed as an individual responsibility, while educational pathways have become more competitive. At the same time, social media can amplify processes of social comparison, putting young people’s achievements, appearance and lifestyles under constant public scrutiny. For many, there is little respite from the pressure to perform.

Economic concerns add another level of pressure. Rising living costs, high tertiary education expanses and uncertainty about future employment rank among young people’s greatest worries. Across the EU, 40% are highly concerned by rising prices and the cost of living. In 2026, national surveys show that around 70% of Irish adolescents consider emigration for better life conditions. Over 20% of Dutch secondary school students are concerned whether they will ever be able to afford a home.
A warming planet and an uncertain future

Today’s young people are growing up amid an increasingly visible climate crisis. They hear repeated warnings about the short- and long-term consequences of climate change. Their generation will be disproportionally affected, and they know it.

For some, this contributes to feelings of anxiety, worry, sadness, anger and helplessness about environmental degradation and the future. Concerns like this about a genuine global threat can be a rational and entirely understandable response.

What can make these concerns particularly difficult is the perception that the decisions affecting young people’s future are often made without their meaningful involvement or consideration of their needs. This cycle of intergenerational injustice needs to be acknowledged and addressed. When people feel they have little influence on issues that will meaningfully shape their lives, this can lead to frustration.

Evidence from many countries suggest that Gen Z are experiencing poorer mental health than previous generations. Although patterns vary across cultures and contexts, large scale studies point to increasing levels of emotional distress and psychological difficulties among young people.

Public discussions often focus on explanations at an individual level: excessive screen time, reduced resilience and difficulties coping with everyday challenges. While these factors may play a role, they do not account for the whole story.

Mental health is shaped by the interaction between individual experiences and wider social, economic and cultural environments in which people live. As such, the current rise in mental health difficulties should not be understood as a solely individual problem. Rather, it reflects a response to broader societal pressures that young people face as they move towards adulthood.

Despite these challenges, it would be wrong to portray Gen Z as a generation defined only by anxiety or pessimism. Protests concerning housing, education, climate policy and economic inequality can express frustration, but they also demonstrate agency and a desire to influence decisions about the future.

A 2025 survey of 6,703 young people across Europe found that 80% of young respondents in Germany considered EU membership a good thing, up from 65% in 2024. In France, the figure rose from 53% to 60%. The study also highlighted the importance young people attach to making the cost of living affordable.

These findings challenge the assumption that today’s young generation is simply disengaged from society. Young people are not passive recipients of social pressures. They organise, question existing arrangements and seek alternatives.

The difficulties facing Gen Z are not entirely new. What makes their experience distinctive is the combination of pressures and the uncertainty surrounding the transition to adulthood. Rather than asking whether today’s young people have it harder than previous generations, we should ask more productive questions: what kind of society are we asking them to navigate? And what can be done to make it healthier, fairer and more hopeful?

articles.title: Hokusai’s Great Wave is one of 46 prints of Mount Fuji – seeing them together changes everything
articles.author: Dominik Havsteen-Franklin, Professor of Arts Psychotherapies & Creative Health, Brunel University of London
paras: When I first saw Katsushika Hokusai’s Clear Day with a Southern Breeze (also known as Red Fuji, 1830-1833), I was struck by its lustrous red resonating against the receding blue of the sky. Clouds align gently in an almost humorous formation. Near the peak of the mountain, are creases of snow. At its foot we are drawn to a multitude of tiny trees amassed in chorus. Easy to overlook, they change the picture. The great mountain becomes itself in relation to everything that surrounds it.

Dulwich Picture Gallery is showing all of Hokusai’s 36 Views of Mount Fuji, including ten added after the series became popular. Hokusai made them in his seventies in the early 1830s as cheap prints for ordinary people in Edo (today’s Tokyo). It is the first, and perhaps only, time the complete series will be shown together in the UK.

One image is instantly recognisable: The Great Wave (actually titled Under the Wave off Kanagawa). Seen alongside the others, it becomes one view among many – and a lesson in how quickly we settle on a single view of anything, including each other.

Three versions of Mount Fuji hang together in the first room. In Red Fuji the mountain is almost pure form. A light blue variant, its ridge edged in heavy indigo, opens a way into the mountain. A third, with lightning like cracks in a pot, feels dark and unsettled.

On the opposite wall hangs The Great Wave. Its foam reaches out like grasping, knuckled fingers, and flecks scatter across the dark water like stars in the night. Everything should be in motion, yet the print holds a stillness. Beneath the wave is Fuji again: a tiny triangle here where Red Fuji’s was expansive. It is the same mountain, but now framed by the sea.

Elsewhere, people hurry over bridges, work in fields and travel along roads. Hills seem to wear patterned bandanas of farmland, while Prussian blue skies fade at a soft, feathered edge. Shapes mingle playfully: three haystacks echo the three small peaks of Fuji’s summit. Hokusai places us in between, looking down on people and up at the sky, but never from a position that reveals everything.

In the third room, one print stopped me. In Mishima Pass in Kai Province, travellers link arms around an enormous tree. I saw an affectionate embrace, then learned they may be measuring its girth. How quickly I had decided what these strangers felt.

As an art psychotherapist, I work with exactly this. We imagine what others might be thinking and feeling, drawing on our own experience – therapists call this mentalising, and doing it well means staying with curiosity rather than assuming we know. I have never been to Japan and cannot experience Fuji as Hokusai’s first viewers did. What reaches me is what colour, form and shape do, across that distance.

Hokusai’s giant tree also recalls an experiment on awe in which people who had gazed up at towering eucalyptus trees for a minute picked up more of a researcher’s “accidentally” dropped pens than those who had looked at a building. A print may not make us kinder, but when we do feel part of a bigger picture, we may just become a bit less absorbed in ourselves, and perhaps more open to others.

The curation is less subtle than the prints. Its dusky blue walls echo Hokusai’s colours, but I was left cold. I felt fixed as a viewer, each picture held apart when I wanted to see how they connect – although the soft lighting creates an atmosphere, a quietness that simply lets you be with them.

At the end of the series, pilgrims climb into Fuji itself. Each looks much like the next, like frames of a stop-motion film. Near the summit they crowd into a shelter in the rock, a small window into something none could enter alone. We no longer look towards a distant mountain; we are drawn into it, among people making their own way upwards.

I left thinking about The Great Wave very differently. I could see the little mountain beneath it, but also the trees, travellers and pilgrims. The Fuji I began with had amassed a sense of journey, unfolding across the series.
Hokusai: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji from the Iuchi Collection is on at Dulwich Picture Gallery, London until January 17, 2027

articles.title: Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z’s weightlifting obsession – here’s why
articles.author: Claire Warden, Professor of Performance and Physical Culture, Loughborough University
paras: More than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out.

Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health.

People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras.
In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry.

As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French.

The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825.

The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century.

A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest.

But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted.

From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa.

Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training.
Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic.
Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake.
The post-war aerobics boom

The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity.

In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom.

New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing.
The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room.

In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it.
Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible.

Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies.
Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics.

By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok.

Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema.
Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm.

articles.title: A critical flaw affecting 70% of all websites has the cybersecurity world panicked
articles.author: Andrew Cullen, Guest Research Fellow, School of Computing and Information Systems, The University of Melbourne
paras: Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline.

The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.
The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time.

PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes.

The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites.
PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it.

In August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase.
The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet.
Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web.
Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix.
In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit.
This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready.
Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule.

Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix.
Why does this keep happening?
Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding.

Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data.

Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations. All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital.
Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is.

This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security.

For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days.
Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning.
Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call.

Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on.

Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening.
Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the World Intellectual Property Organizations AI Technical Exchange Committee, and the managing consultant at EthiCan.

articles.title: Protest as a pillar of democracy
articles.author: Malka Older
paras: Protest helps close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we actually have
Originally published on Global Voices

This piece is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Democracy is often presented as an orderly, structured system of representation and deliberation, colorless and linear like an organizational version of the faux-classical architecture so many democratic countries adopt for their government buildings. Voting leads to representatives, debates lead to votes on laws, participation leads to action, like columns leading to a pediment.

But democracy is not actually about cushy debating chambers or political speeches — or not only about that. Democracy means rule by the people, and in most of the systems we call democracies today, the people’s role is for the most part narrowed to voting, and often a curtailed, difficult, limited vote that does little for accountability or expressing preferences on specific issues.

Protest is one of the ways we close the gap between the promise of democracy and the formal structures we have. With protest, the people can express general emotional responses or very specific policy proposals; we can punctuate the long intervals of electoral cycles to influence government outside of the voting booth; and perhaps most importantly, we build coalitions and solidarity, forming a collective consciousness of our democratic responsibilities.

Voting is a single, standardized, and fairly isolated action. Protest, on the other hand, unfolds in dozens, if not hundreds, of permutations, letting us — the people — express our creativity along with our civic engagement. One of the wonderful things about this spotlight has been seeing the sheer range of capacity and ingenuity as people use protest to inspire others, express anger or determination, and pressure governments and other decision-makers.

Maybe the most obvious example of this in the spotlight is the collaborative article on protest music, with its examples of not just different songs, but different styles and approaches and even understanding of what it means to use music for advocacy. In Japan, young people are finding new paths into activism, like handing out placards, while the Cockroach Janta Party in India has used memes and online jokes to mobilize young people right from the start of the movement.

Severe oppression requires more creativity, as this article about the evolution of street art in Russia points out. Similarly, Russians — many of them in exile — used allusion and wordplay in online videos to get their messages across.

That raises the question, ably explored in this piece, about whether online and offline protest are equally effective, and what their different strengths and weaknesses are. And, if the digital world has enabled new forms of protest, it has also activated new means of repression. Our friends at Ranking Digital Rights contributed this well-researched article about the complicity of telecoms in internet shutdowns in Africa. This piece, from AlgorithmWatch, details the Russian surveillance software being used against protesters in Georgia. And the virtual world can be used to hijack, undermine, or redirect protest energy, as this case study from Funky Citizens in Romania details.

As vibrant as protests are in the moment, though, it’s also important to ask about the long-term impact, the consequences, both good and bad. The protests in Bangladesh two years ago were successful in the sense that they led to a change of government; this article asks whether that change of government led to a meaningful difference in democratic accountability. And this powerful piece from Nepal follows up with those involved in the Gen Z protests there last year, tracking the long-term impacts of injuries and trauma.

As with all our monthly spotlights, this one is in many ways about showing the common threads that link all of our countries, as well as the exceptions that can open us to new ideas or inspire us to a different kind of action. This spotlight is, then, a form of protest in its own right: a way of reasserting that protest is legitimate, important for democracy, and everywhere.

articles.title: Palestine is already living under the Big Tech authoritarianism the world is being sold
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: Emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control
Originally published on Global Voices
An aerial view showing destruction in Rafah, Gaza Strip, on January 21, 2025. Photo by Ashraf Amra on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO).

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For Palestinians, the relationship between technology and authoritarianism is a lived reality, rather than predictions or science fiction. Israel’s settler-colonial regime has long fused military force with legal, economic and technological mechanisms to dominate Palestinian life.

Surveillance, data harvesting, facial recognition, telecommunications blackouts, digital censorship and algorithmic systems are now woven into this architecture of control. The genocidal war on Gaza has exposed the consequences with devastating clarity, where technologies built to collect, process and classify information have been absorbed into systems that surveil, target and kill Palestinians.

But Palestine is also a warning about what comes next. Technologies developed, tested and refined under occupation do not stay there. They become products, expertise and business models that circulate globally. What emerges is a political economy in which military and intelligence institutions, technology companies, investors and governments converge around the extraction and processing of data as a means of exercising power.

This is one of the central arguments of Digital Domination, a publication of The Arab Center for the Advancement of Social Media’s Maryam Abu Daqqa Fellowship, which brings together five studies on artificial intelligence, surveillance, data extraction and corporate power in Palestine and beyond. The fellowship is named after Maryam Abu Daqqa, a Palestinian journalist murdered by Israel in Gaza in August 2025 while documenting life under siege. Across different cases, the research points to the same transformation, showing how emerging technologies have become central to systems of coercion and control. It is becoming their infrastructure.

Israel’s surveillance industry shows this plainly. It operates through intimate ties between military and intelligence institutions, private companies, venture capital and international markets. Tools tested on Palestinians are refined, repackaged as commercial products and exported to the world as security solutions. This is no accident of a thriving tech sector. It is a political and economic system in which security technologies gain value precisely because of their capacity to monitor, classify and control populations.

The violence these systems enable is increasingly literal. Investigations into Israel’s AI-assisted targeting systems, including Lavender, The Gospel and Where’s Daddy, have documented how machine-learning systems and mass surveillance data have been folded into the identification and targeting of Palestinians in Gaza.

A new film, NAZA, produced by The Guardian and built on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, details the secret systems used to select people for bombing in their homes at night, in the knowledge that their families would be killed, too. At a military conference in London in late June, an executive from the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems presented a slide crediting its digital command system with 850,000 “real-time intel targets” across Gaza and Lebanon between October 2023 and the end of 2025. The company has since tried to recast the figure as aggregate system activity, a claim that sits uneasily with the slide itself.

The significance is not that an algorithm has replaced human violence. It is that these systems increase the scale, speed and bureaucratic distance at which violence is organised, while cloaking life-and-death decisions in the appearance of technical objectivity. In June, Amnesty International and more than 100 other signatories warned that systems such as Lavender, Gospel and Where’s Daddy dilute human responsibility and obscure international crimes behind a veneer of algorithmic objectivity.

The same architecture extends beyond weapons. At 7amleh, we have documented how platforms suppress Palestinian speech, how state-linked actors use commercial platforms to shape information environments, and how Meta profits from content and accounts tied to illegal settlement expansion and violent rhetoric against Palestinians.

Two studies in Digital Domination make the point from different angles. One examines the Israeli government’s use of Google advertising to place its preferred narratives in front of people searching for information. Another examines algorithmic voice surveillance, showing how Palestinian speech itself is captured as data for systems of control.

This is where digital erasure becomes inseparable from physical violence. The destruction of Gaza also threatens the evidence and memory through which Palestinians can establish what was done to them. Platforms have removed or restricted documentation of Israeli violence, while physical archives, cultural records, cemeteries and the evidence beneath Gaza’s rubble have been destroyed or put at risk.

The UN refugee agency UNRWA ran a covert 10-month operation to smuggle millions of documents out of Gaza and East Jerusalem, amid fears that the originals, and even their digital copies, could be seized or destroyed. This September, the UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, warned that Israel’s clearance of Gaza’s rubble could destroy evidence of atrocity crimes, and called it unacceptable that Gaza’s reconstruction be conditioned on the erasure of its past and the evidence needed to secure justice for its victims.

The problem, therefore, goes far beyond whether a post stays online. It concerns who retains the power to document reality, preserve history and establish evidence after violence has taken place. We have described this wider process as platformicide: the destruction and denial of the digital spaces through which Palestinians communicate, organise, document and preserve collective memory.
Now the same problem is entering the systems through which people increasingly access knowledge.

Large language models and AI agents are becoming intermediaries between people and information, yet they are acutely vulnerable to manipulation. Microsoft’s security researchers have documented “AI recommendation poisoning,” in which companies embed hidden instructions that plant persistent biases in AI assistants’ memory, with 31 companies across 14 industries identified.

Salesforce researchers found that web-search agents fed authoritative-looking false content will reproduce it as fact: in controlled tests, around 80 percent of queries returned the attacker’s preferred answer, and in more realistic conditions, with poisoned documents buried among more than 100,000 clean ones, nearly one in four did.

For Palestine, this is not hypothetical. Drop Site News reported that Israel awarded a USD 46.5 million contract to Brad Parscale’s firm Clock Tower X to build networks of websites and blog posts aimed at shaping what chatbots tell users about Gaza, content written for machines rather than readers. Journalists have since put leading chatbots to the test to see how far the campaign has reached.

A society already subjected to censorship, propaganda, data extraction and the destruction of evidence is now entering an information environment in which people increasingly depend on AI systems to tell them what is true, what happened and what matters, and in which the party responsible for the violence is paying to shape those answers.

The danger is not only inaccurate information. It is the concentration of epistemic power in systems whose training data, retrieval mechanisms and decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Information manipulation can move from suppressing a Palestinian post to shaping what an AI system retrieves, remembers, or presents as knowledge.

Meanwhile, the technologies and companies enabling these systems are becoming embedded in public life elsewhere. In the UK, Palantir’s GBP 330 million National Health Service (NHS) contract led a parliamentary committee to call the company’s growing public-sector role “an unacceptable point of weakness”, and the government is now reviewing the contract amid pressure to use a break clause in 2027. In the United States, Amnesty International has documented how technology from Palantir and Babel Street is used to monitor and target migrants and people speaking out for Palestinian rights.

These developments should be understood as part of a wider transformation in how power is organised. Palestine shows what happens when data, surveillance infrastructure, artificial intelligence and corporate power are integrated into systems of domination. It also shows how quickly technologies developed in one context travel into another, stripped of the political conditions of their making and repackaged as innovation, efficiency, security or digital transformation.

The authoritarianism of the digital age does not require every state to build its own surveillance apparatus. It can purchase one. It does not require governments to control every source of information. It can outsource the infrastructure through which information is filtered, ranked and delivered. It does not require violence to disappear from public view. It can make violence more scalable, more automated and harder to attribute.
Palestinians are already living with the consequences. The rest of the world should heed the warning before these systems become too deeply embedded in its own institutions to challenge.

articles.title: When Big Tech becomes a tool of state control in Kenya
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: State censorship on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them
Originally published on Global Voices
Image of person using Telegram by Christian Wiediger via Unsplash (Free to use). Image of Kenyan flag by User:Pumbaa80 via Wikimedia Commons(Public domain). Illustration by Global Voices.

This post by Grace Kobare is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

On January 30, 2018, Raila Odinga held his symbolic “swearing-in” ceremony in Nairobi, and the government, through Kenya’s regulator, switched off the transmitters of KTN, NTV and Citizen TV while they were broadcasting live.
The Interior Ministry defended the move, saying the media had been given a security briefing in advance. The stations stayed off air for days and were only fully back by February 9, 2018.
Kenya's internet freedom drops drastically

The 2018 incident was just one of many examples of Kenyan officials cutting off connectivity — particularly during times of unrest. During the June 2024 tax protests, authorities shut down internet connectivity for around seven hours and arrested a large number of protesters. The Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) also reported that at least three networks blocked the web version of Telegram during those protests, and the blocks were reversed the same day.

A year later, during the June 2025 protests throughout Kenya, a communications authority issued a directive to media houses to stop live broadcasts of the unrest, and Telegram was blocked again. Access Now said this violated a High Court injunction against interfering with internet and Telegram access.

Given these incidents, it is no surprise that Kenya’s internet freedom record has worsened in recent years. Freedom House found that in 2025 Kenya had the most severe decline of the 72 countries assessed during the coverage period.
A wider pattern of internet freedom decline

Kenya’s experience is part of a wider pattern. Freedom House found that global internet freedom declined for the 15th consecutive year in 2025, as authoritarian governments used censorship and offline repression to crush protests organized online. Access Now’s 2025 report found that at least 313 shutdowns were implemented globally, and that in Africa the internet was shut down 30 times in 15 countries, with protests the leading trigger, followed by elections.

In Tanzania, an internet blackout was imposed after protests erupted on election day, October 29, 2025. It was only partially eased on November 4, alongside a curfew. An opposition lawyer said online mobilization was part of the reason for the blanket block, and protesters used VPNs to reach platforms such as X Spaces.

In Uganda, the regulator ordered all mobile operators and internet providers to suspend public internet access nationwide from 6 p.m. on 13 January 2026, two days before the general election. Officials had publicly denied plans for a blanket shutdown beforehand. The platforms themselves have been targets too: A Facebook ban followed the five-day blackout of the 2021 election and was still in effect in 2026, and Starlink disabled its terminals in the country after Uganda ordered the service shut down on grounds they were unlicensed.
Kenya’s case shows how state pressure on information has moved from broadcasters to platforms and the laws that govern them.
Checks through Kenya’s courts
The June 2025 Telegram block came despite a High Court injunction. The government has also tried to write that power into law.

In October 2025, President William Ruto signed the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act. Human Rights Watch (HRW) said it risks criminalizing legitimate online speech. The Act also expanded the powers of a state committee, the National Computer and Cybercrimes Coordination Committee (NC4), to make websites and apps inaccessible.

The High Court in Nairobi suspended key sections a week after Ruto signed it. By July 2026, the High Court had declared the website-blocking powers unconstitutional. The chairperson of the Bloggers Association of Kenya, Kennedy Kachwanya, told Human Rights Watch that the amended law poses an unacceptable threat to digital rights and freedom of expression.
Beyond individual platforms

Amnesty International documented a coordinated campaign between June 2024 and July 2025 that used social media and digital tools to suppress Gen Z-led protests in Kenya. Amnesty found that X was central to pro-government networks, as pro-government actors posted identical messages repeatedly to hijack the platform’s algorithm and sway public perception. Amnesty noted that X failed to act on organized campaigns that violate its own policy. A participant told Amnesty he was part of a network of around 20 people paid roughly KES 25,000 (USD 192.50) to KES 50,000 (USD 385.29) a day to push pro-government messages onto X’s trending lists.

The Kenyan government is now seeking more direct leverage over big tech companies. The ICT Cabinet Secretary told the Senate that X must open a physical office in Kenya within three months or lose operating approval. The directive extends to TikTok and Meta, and gives the communications authority powers to suspend non-compliant platforms. The government framed this as a move to protect children online. However, a rights group summary of the move cautions that local presence could let authorities pressure staff and demand takedowns quietly.

Kenya’s courts have so far pushed back on some of the harshest measures, but the pressure keeps changing, from switching off television in 2018, to disrupting internet access in 2024 and blocking Telegram in 2025, and now to demands that platforms set up offices in the country.

What happens next depends partly on the companies themselves. They can resist orders that silence their users, or they can decide that keeping access to the Kenyan market is worth complying with the government’s demands. For Kenyans who rely on these platforms to organize and to be heard, that choice matters, because it helps decide how much of their public conversation stays free from state control.

articles.title: The problem with Shane Gillis’s joke isn’t just sexism, it’s sex work stigma
articles.author: Carmen Logie, Full Professor, Factor-Inwentash Faculty of Social Work, University of Toronto
paras: In his Oct. 10 Saturday Night Live (SNL) monologue, American comedian Shane Gillis joked that women at the gym dress like “whores” these days. The backlash was swift and widespread, in the news and across social media. Critics zeroed in on the sexualization of women who are simply trying to exercise without being harassed or judged.

While that’s fair, much of the criticism overlooked another problem. The objections often came down to this: these women aren’t sex workers, so they shouldn’t be called “whores.” That response leaves the insult itself intact, along with the assumption that being compared to a sex worker is degrading.

However well-intentioned, Canadian actor Dan Levy, for example, argued on Instagram only that wearing short shorts to the gym doesn’t make women “whores,” it makes the men calling them that misogynists.

The normalization of stigma toward sex workers runs deep. Everyday language, media coverage and public conversations all contribute to stigmatizing attitudes toward sex workers and to social norms that can fuel discrimination and exclusion. When we object to women being called “whores,” we can unintentionally reinforce the idea that being compared to a sex worker is an insult.
Gillis also joked about looking lesbian and gay, adding homophobia to the mix. Sex work stigma and homophobia have this in common: both are rooted in ideas of sexual immorality and deviance.
Stigma toward sex workers matters

Sex workers around the world experience profound health and social inequities. A recent series in The Lancet Public Health documents their disproportionate exposure to violence, unsafe working conditions and poor health outcomes. The series traces these sustained inequities to stigma and the criminalization of sex work.

Canada is no exception. Canada’s sex work laws, such as the Protection of Communities and Exploited Persons Act (PCEPA), criminalize purchasing sexual services even though selling one’s own sexual services generally is not.

This can make it harder for sex workers to screen potential clients because it limits how they can communicate with them and negotiate their safety. For instance, clients may be reluctant to share their identifying information due to fear of being arrested, in turn making it harder for sex workers to verify their identity, check references and learn about potentially dangerous clients.

Fear of police surveillance can also drive sexual transactions into more isolated settings, making it harder for sex workers to access help if needed. Criminalizing third-party involvement can also create barriers to safety arrangements, such as working with others to screen clients.
But why is calling a woman a “whore” still considered an insult?
Where the stigma comes from

In his 1963 book Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity, sociologist Erving Goffman described stigma as a social process through which certain people are labelled and discredited. Among them were people judged as “immoral,” like sex workers and lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer people.
But stigma is more than a set of negative attitudes. It’s also about power: who has access to resources and opportunities, who is valued and who is seen as deserving of dignity and respect.

Feminist scholar Gail Pheterson explored how this plays out for women in her work on “whore stigma” more than 30 years ago. She argued that the label “whore” is used to control women’s sexuality by sorting women into groups of those considered respectable and those judged immoral, dishonourable or sexually deviant.

It’s crucial to note that a woman does not even have to be a sex worker to be labelled a “whore.” Any woman perceived as violating gendered expectations of how to dress, act or express her sexuality can be.

This brings us back to Gillis’s joke. The women at the gym are not being called “whores” because their occupation is to sell sex. Gillis uses sex work as shorthand for sexual deviance. The joke only works if being compared to a sex worker is accepted as degrading. And this is the problem.

In other words, it is possible to challenge the sexism reflected in the policing of some women’s bodies and still overlook the gender-based stigma toward the women whose identities are being used as an insult.
The connection to homophobia

Gillis’s jokes about looking gay or lesbian draw on the same logic. While homophobia and stigma toward sex workers have distinct histories, both are rooted in social expectations about whose sexuality is considered acceptable.

Researchers call the devaluation of people based on same-gender attraction, identities, relationships and practices “sexual stigma.” It extends well beyond insults and negative attitudes. Sexual stigma shapes laws, health care, employment, opportunities and social relationships. It also limits people’s ability to live safely and openly, with dignity and full rights.
Multiple forms of stigma can also intersect. Queer sex workers, for example, may face stigma and discrimination related to both their sexual identity and their occupation.
Reclaiming a slur versus using one
A joke premised on the idea that being gay, lesbian or a sex worker is embarrassing or shameful does more than fall flat. It reproduces wider social beliefs about who’s acceptable and who’s not.

Interestingly, some sex workers have reclaimed the term “whore” to resist stigma and express pride. But there is a difference between a marginalized community reclaiming a stigmatizing label and outsiders using it to demean.
The backlash against Gillis’s SNL monologue raises an important question: can we challenge the policing of women’s bodies without reinforcing stigma toward sex workers?
We can — and we should. Women deserve to exercise without being sexualized, judged or harassed. Sex workers deserve the same dignity, safety and respect.

When we fight against women being called “whores,” we should ask whether we are mainly concerned because these women aren’t sex workers. This becomes a problem if it means accepting that a sex worker is someone unworthy of respect.
What we need to talk about more as a society is not just that women at the gym are being compared to sex workers. It’s that being compared to a sex worker continues to be used as an insult.

articles.title: French students are showing us what protest looks like in the age of viral spectacle
articles.author: Sara García Santamaría, Assistant Professor in Journalism Studies, Universitat de València
paras: The recent wave of protests in Europe have left us with two striking, viral spectacles of violence and joy. As Limoges’ historic town hall went up in flames, the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde was playing classical music in Paris’ central Place de la République (until the musicians were teargassed by police, that is).

Both scenes offer radically different ways of seeing the protests. The burning town hall offers a powerful image of destruction; the orchestra, of anti-authoritarian collective solidarity. Neither tells the whole story, but their contrast raises important questions: which image will come to represent the protests, and who decides what we see?

France’s demonstrations began with students protesting deteriorating school conditions, including staff shortages and dilapidated buildings. But they quickly intersected with broader anger over living costs and public services.

The unrest also formed part of a wider European moment. On the same weekend, people took to the streets in Spain, Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Albania. Grievances include low wages, rising energy prices and unaffordable housing, each within its own national context.

These were separate mobilisations, not a single coordinated movement. Yet they reveal how different struggles are being represented in an age where everything – including a mass protest movement – can go viral.
The battle over meaning starts with language.
On October 19, the European Commission condemned looting as “unacceptable” while stressing that peaceful protest must be protected.

In the European Parliament, the centre-right European People’s Party, backed by the European Conservatives and Reformists, has framed the unrest as an ideological threat, proposing a debate titled “France, Italy and Belgium: Latest anti-democratic violence by radical far-left groups”.

These interventions reflect a broader contest over whether demonstrations should be understood primarily as expressions of social grievances, or as challenges to public order. Political leaders across Europe have sought to steer this debate.
In France and Italy, Emmanuel Macron and Giorgia Meloni distinguished between people’s right to demonstrate and violent delinquents.

However, other politicians such as French far-right leader Marine Le Pen have blamed the far left and immigrants. In Spain, Madrid’s regional leader Isabel Díaz Ayuso pointed to the “anti-democratic left”, while Albania’s socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama described the protesters as being radicalised by “antifa”.

The name we give to these gatherings – rally, riot, protest – matters greatly, as it shapes public and policy perceptions of what is legitimate in democratic societies. This, in turn, decides what kind of response – in particular what level of violence and repression – people will accept in addressing them.

Disruptive protests are typically presented negatively in both political discourse and in the mainstream media, regardless of an outlet’s political stance. This happens by connecting protest to violence, ideological extremism and threats to democratic legitimacy, thus discrediting protesters and their demands.

This means isolated violence can come to represent an entire demonstration or movement. On October 17, over half a million protesters took to the streets across France, but these historic, peaceful demonstrations have been completely eclipsed by media coverage of the looting that ensued.
Leer más: France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest

At Place de la République, the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde brought together hundreds of musicians to play popular, well-known pieces like the anti-fascist anthem Bella Ciao, along with songs from The Avengers and The Hunger Games.

The concert did not, of course, make the conflict disappear. What it offered was another way to see it, not simply as a confrontation between police and disorderly crowds, but as a collective performance of resistance.

Gen Z’s cultural symbols have also played a key role in generating viral spectacles. In France, students have appeared dressed as Batman, Chucky and other anime characters. People have protested dressed up as Pepe the Frog or holding the One Piece pirate flag, connecting Europe’s demonstrations to the symbols of global Gen Z protests, from Portland to Kathmandu.
Leer más: From anime to activism: How the ‘One Piece’ pirate flag became the global emblem of Gen Z resistance

Some students attending the October 17 protests told Le Monde “there’s no point in getting angry, so we might as well do it with a smile”. And that is precisely the point: both memes and spectacle can put joy, humour and playfulness at the centre, making grievances visible on the protesters’ own terms and generating viral images that compete with negative media coverage.

The fire in Limoges and the orchestra in Paris are not competing truths, and neither should cancel the other out. What these events have in common is the framing of protests as viral spectacles, staged for the cameras, digital platforms and distant audiences.

A burning building and a massive concert are easy to capture on camera, while struggles over housing, the cost of living and the deterioration of public services are not. Understanding protest therefore means looking beyond the image that travels furthest, fastest and most easily. It means asking who selected them, and whose account they serve when they go viral.
