articles.title: France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest
articles.author: Paolo Stuppia, Sociologue, membre du CESSP (Centre Européen de Sociologie et de Science Politique), Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne
paras: Following widespread looting sprees and acts of violence occurring on the sidelines of the October 17 student protests, so-called “casseurs” seem to be the centre of attention. But the term, which comes from the French verb casser or “to break”, poses more questions than answers. The sociologist Paolo Stuppia examines the unprecedented situation many cities across France are having to contend with, and the complex combination of collective action whose motivations are unclear and the social media’s extreme agility.
The Conversation: How unprecedented are the scenes of looting that we witnessed on the sidelines of the October 17 demonstrations?

Paolo Stuppia: What may be unprecedented is the extent of the destruction of private property and the goods that have been stolen. It should be clear, however, that not all the looters can necessarily be sorted into identifiable groups, at least politically.

Indeed, as the politician Xavier Crettiez, the sociologist Isabelle Sommier and the historian François Audigier emphasised in 2021 in their joint project Violences politiques en France, the targets of acts of violence that are considered to be politically motivated can be determined both by technical constraints and the militant culture of the people involved. Let us recall Italy in the 1970s when autonomous activists spoke of “self-reduction” (the act of seizing goods or essential services), Maoists in France spoke of proletarian reappropriation. Their raid on Fauchon’s luxury grocery store on place de la madeleine and the redistribution of goods to slums and workers’ hostels that ensued went down in history as their biggest claim to fame.

Can we go as far as to say that the October 17 looting sprees were politically motivated? Even if we do not have all the details concerning the profiles of the people arrested, videos posted on social media and stolen goods being resold online tend to rule out the idea. That said, at least some of the targets were chosen haphazardly. While some are symbols of capitalism, like luxury stores, insurance companies, banks, multinationals, others included a number of more localised stores, small shops selling toys or video games; for example, which are rarely targets for such incidents.

If, especially since the alter-globalisation movement, we have seen the emergence of damage to property, primarily targeting symbols of capitalism and multinationals, in particular; this phenomenon goes hand in hand with “off the cuff” incidents by groups without any political affiliation, who join demonstrations to “get in on the act” in such a way that we are unable to determine whether it’s just a way of letting off steam or if it’s driven by a goal of redistributing goods – this weekend we witnessed some scenes of goods being redistributed, such as food being given to the homeless.
What do we know about casseurs’ profiles? When did they appear in the demonstrations and when did the term first appear in the media?

P.S.: Historically, the first research article on the casseur phenomenon can be traced back to the sociologist Gwenola Ricordeau. In France in the 1990s, as was the case during the student and high school movement of 1998, Ricordeau noticed that young people came to demonstrations to commit acts of vandalism or to mug people without having anything to do with the causes behind protest movements. They were driven by opportunism and also a desire to break up the monotony of everyday life.

The fact of disqualifying people by designating them as “criminals on the street” therefore ultimately leads us to riot-like phenomena, with or without the “looting” element, which are part of the continuity of “suburban revolt” or “city riots” which have gradually developed in working-class neighbourhoods since the second half of the 1970s. As we demonstrated alongside the sociologist Valérie Becquet in our book Géopolitique de la jeunesse, it forms a collection of pejorative and disqualifying terms pertaining to a so-called “dangerous youth”.

The term “casseur”, along with the derogatory term “racaille”, an old French term meaning rabble for example, widely resonated in the language of the media during the 2005 unrest to refer to a lumpenproletariat of young people who attacked both police and vandalised private property and a number of public services and property or street furniture, but whose actions were void of any political meaning.

If we take the theory of labelling, we can understand that the term “casseurs” is linked to the stigma attached to young people from working-class neighbourhoods. But there can also be a second meaning: the phenomena in which France’s Mouvance autonome (a movement drawing its influences from anarchism and situationism that sets itself apart), is involved in scenes of outbreaks of violence and damage to property, even harm targeting individuals. However, we should first note that the movement has a history of claiming responsibility for its actions. The casseur stigma is also turned around and sometimes used with self-derision.

In 2006, during the protests over contrat première embauche or first job contract law, there were tensions between those who said “we aren’t” or “we don’t want casseurs”, others who said, “it’s the government and the employers – they are the casseurs”. And it was in this context that a banner that appeared in Rennes (in western France), ended up in Paris, claiming: “We are all casseurs.” As if to recognise the term for what it is: a historically vague label, covering different realities, and that the media has invited to every protest movement without fail over the past 30 years.

It’s a bit like the expression “black bloc”: “casseurs” is used to refer to people who resort to techniques that are out of order or who conjure up a considerable cause for concern among a certain part of public opinion, and yet the term remains very vague and is easily instrumentalised.
How is social media a gamechanger for law enforcement?

P.S.: There is a clear difference between fairly structured protest movements, even in an informal way, and the much more spontaneous use of social networks to stage action among young and very young people, such as filming themselves wearing football shirts as they leave Paris’ Place de la République.

We are facing a generation that is demonstrating a certain digital agility. There is a proliferation of platforms. In the days of the yellow vests, we were still largely using tools that came from the Internet of the 2000s, whether it was Instagram, Facebook, a bit of messaging, but not that much, and also Twitter. What we are now seeing is a new wave of social networks in action, with tools also designed to reduce control, like Snapchat, or Telegram, where content is extremely short-lived.

The question would then be: how do we adapt to these new ways of using social media? There is also the phenomenon of loops, which are difficult to infiltrate, with people who move very quickly and provide real-time support for those involved in the movements, on a rather confidential level. One of the hypotheses would be that, in this case, law enforcement is a bit helpless.

There is a quickfire of information, several levels of conversation, with public and private chatrooms, and more or less restricted groups. These real-time conversations are much more difficult to apprehend. Beyond messages that rapidly disappear on Snapchat, for example, a whole set of parameters specific to this universe must be taken into account: profiles feature scores related to the person’s activity; anyone who infiltrates is therefore almost immediately identifiable.

The combination of extremely agile social media and protesters’ mobility is very difficult to control. An example of this was the youth movements in Hong Kong in 2019-2020, which caused a lot of trouble for the authorities, even though it involved a police force with a tutelary government that could still be called authoritarian. Even they struggled to control the groups of young demonstrators operating via social networks, committing fragmented acts, with ten people in one place, ten at another, dispersing quickly. It makes you wonder how much of an information time lapse we are contending with . But that will be up to the parliamentary commission of inquiry to work out.

articles.title: Africa’s bats could survive climate change – if they can find somewhere to live
articles.author: Mariëtte van der Walt, Biodiversity Coordinator, Wilderness, University of the Witwatersrand
paras: Climate change and changes in the way land is used are the two biggest threats to wildlife because they change the environment in which animals survive and thrive. Knowing how species respond to these pressures is central to planning conservation actions.
A number of studies have modelled how climate change will affect vertebrate distributions. But little is known about bats from tropical and subtropical regions, especially in Africa.

Bats are particularly sensitive to changes to their environment because of their slow reproductive rates, dependence on stable roosts, and sensitivity to climatic extremes that shape insect availability – their main source of food.

They therefore need both suitable foraging landscapes and the availability of caves for roosting. Research has been done on how bats will be affected by the effects of climate change such as rising temperatures. What has been overlooked is the fact that cave-dependent bats can’t survive in climatically suitable areas without access to suitable roosts.

So even if a future landscape has the right temperature and rainfall, it may be of little use to a bat if there is nowhere suitable to roost. That led us to a simple question: what happens when the places with the right climate aren’t the places with caves?

Having studied bats since 2017, I have spent much of my research career investigating their ecology and dependence on particular habitats. This experience led me to question where climate change might push wildlife. I wanted to understand whether Africa’s cave-dwelling bats would actually be able to find somewhere to live as the climate changes.

My co-author Mark Keith and I set out to answer this by building a model that brought together future climate conditions and the availability of caves and rocky roosting habitat across sub-Saharan Africa. We used cave-dwelling long-fingered bats called Miniopteridae as our study group to explore how these two essential pieces of the puzzle might overlap in the future.

Long-fingered bats are found widely across Africa and depend heavily on caves for shelter. They also commonly occur alongside other cave-dwelling bat species, making them a useful group for understanding how climate change could affect bats that rely on caves.

Our findings suggest that Africa’s cave-dwelling bats face a double challenge. Climate change could shrink the areas where they can live, but even where future conditions remain suitable, there might not be caves.
Places need to found where three things come together: the climate remains suitable; there is somewhere for the bats to live; and they can move between the places they need.
These could become critical safe havens for bats as the climate changes.
Modelling where bats can survive

We used an existing database of 551 reliable records showing where these bats have been found across sub-Saharan Africa. We then used these records to ask where conditions could remain suitable for them as the climate changes. Using a computer model, we matched each of these places with its local climate, such as how hot, cold or wet it gets, to work out what conditions the bats need. We then asked the model where those conditions would still exist around 2070, if the world carries on warming at a moderate rate.

We found that, depending on how the climate changes in the coming decades, the area with suitable conditions for these bats could shrink by 36% to 64% by 2061-2080. The areas that remained suitable were concentrated mainly in southern Africa, the eastern highlands and Madagascar.
We then went on to answer the next question. Were there caves in those places?

When we compared the areas with a suitable future climate with the locations of suitable caves and rocky landscapes, the picture became much more worrying. Only around 5% of the areas with suitable caves also had a climate expected to remain suitable for the bats. And when we considered how vulnerable the surrounding landscape was to future change, that fell to around 2%.
In other words, the places where bats might find the right climate and the places where they might find a home barely overlapped.

In addition, for some cave-dwelling bats, survival is not simply about finding one suitable cave. They may depend on a network of caves spread across the landscape, moving between them at different times of the year. That means the landscape between caves matters too.

A cave might provide an ideal shelter, but if the surrounding landscape has become heavily fragmented by roads, cities, agriculture or other changes, reaching another suitable cave may become much more difficult. And flying takes energy. If bats have to travel further between places where they can feed, rest and reproduce, they may have to spend more of their limited energy simply getting around. For animals already dealing with a changing climate, that could add another layer of pressure.
A problem that goes beyond bats

Our findings are important for a range of animals. A frog may need a particular wetland. A bird may depend on a particular type of forest. A plant may only grow in a certain kind of soil. As the climate changes, the conditions these species need may shift, but their homes may not.

This creates a challenge for conservation: it is not enough to ask where the climate will be suitable for wildlife in the future. We also need to ask whether wildlife will actually have somewhere to live when it gets there.

articles.title: Japan’s expensive funerals and declining birth rates are transforming ancestral traditions
articles.author: Mimi Hanaoka, Associate Professor of Religious Studies, University of Richmond
paras: Whenever I drive amid the mazelike bustle of Tokyo’s Shuto Expressway, where approximately 1 million vehicles transit daily, I see billboard advertisements for all manner of businesses: dentists, hotels, car and tire companies, and affordable funerals. Lots and lots of funerals.
For generations, Japan’s funeral system rested on family and community networks and Buddhist temples. Together, they sustained the traditional system of burials into the 20th century.

Today, Japan is facing a crisis of funerals and burials. Funerals averaged approximately 1.2 million yen or about US$7,600, according to a 2024 national survey – approximately one-quarter of an average Japanese worker’s annual gross earnings.

Consequently, many Japanese are thinking about whether to continue burial traditions that will place on their children and grandchildren the financial, logistical and emotional costs associated with maintaining the family grave. Japan’s falling birthrate means there are fewer people to care for their ancestors’ graves, which has made the problem more urgent.

As a professor of religion who researches death rituals, I am struck by the innovative death rituals that are emerging in Japan, where I was born and raised. These new rituals reshape some traditions but preserve the importance of remaining connected with the dead.
Japanese funerary rites involve both cremation and burial. First the deceased is cremated, then their bones are buried, typically weeks, months or years after cremation.
Cremation is overwhelmingly standard for Japanese burials today, with between 99.7% and 99.9% of the deceased cremated. In any given year, fewer than 400 people are buried without cremation.

After the deceased is cremated in a coffin, family members place some or most of the bone fragments into a funerary urn. Family members take the urn home to be placed on a Buddhist altar. The bones are later interred in a grave, ossuary or columbarium – “nōkotsudō” – which are permanent structures where bones are interred in compartments.

Traditionally, mourners at Japanese funerals bring a cash gift to offset the cost of funerals. Protocol dictates that the family of the deceased later send return gifts that are worth half the value of the cash gift that was given. These are typically gift boxes of coffee or tea, or elegant but pragmatic items, such as high-quality towels or soaps, sent within a few weeks of the funeral.
Post-death Buddhist rituals are held weekly through the 49th day and then continue periodically, at minimum, until the third death anniversary.

The price for a grave and interment are in addition to the funeral costs. Purchasing a grave means buying the headstone and use of the plot; the temple, municipal cemetery or private cemetery owns the land itself.

In 2025, a gravestone, plot and cemetery-use fees amounted to 1.52 million yen – close to $10,000. The combined costs of an average funeral and average grave are equivalent to almost 60% of of an average worker’s annual salary.

Costs do not end after cremation, funeral and burial. Municipal and private cemeteries charge annual fees for land maintenance. There are additional fees for Buddhist rituals to be performed at the grave, which are believed to benefit the deceased in the afterlife.

Most Tokyo municipal cemeteries charge less than $40 per year. These costs fall on descendants, who also traditionally visit and maintain the grave, make offerings and keep the grave and surrounding area neat and tidy.

Graves can be effectively repossessed by the cemetery or temple if they are abandoned and annual maintenance fees go unpaid. The bones in a repossessed grave are then reinterred in a communal ossuary or columbarium.
Tree burials and other adaptations
The combination of a shrinking population, limited grave plots and costs that continue in perpetuity make alternatives to a traditional grave attractive.

These include “tree burials,” known as “jumokusō,” where the deceased’s bones or ashes are buried in or around a tree. Tree burials are becoming increasingly popular, with a 2022 consumer survey indicating that they account for just over 40% of all new graves.

Two Tokyo Metropolitan public cemeteries now offer “Forest Type” – “Jūrin-gata” – burial, where cremated remains in silk bags are interred into a designated plot of land. A living individual can reserve a burial spot and know that there will be no management fees in perpetuity.

This is in contrast to regular Tokyo Metropolitan public cemeteries’ graves, for which an individual cannot reserve a spot while still alive. Grave plots are first-come, first-served, and since death is unpredictable, graves cannot be reserved in advance.

Some opt for ossuaries and columbariums, which exist in various styles, from more traditional Buddhist altar-style compartments to modern locker-style housing for the urns. There are even automated columbariums, where urns are stored in a centralized system and then retrieved mechanically and placed in a private memorial cubby when a family visits to pay respects to their loved ones. There are also communal ossuaries, where the deceased’s bones are mixed with the bones of others, either immediately or after a certain period of time.
Bone buddhas and other innovations

Arrestingly beautiful but rare are the bone buddhas – “kotsubotoke” – statues of Amida Buddha, or Buddha of Infinite Light. They are made from the partial remains of tens and sometimes hundreds of thousands of individuals’ cremated remains that have been pulverized into fine ash before being compressed into sculptures.

Amida Buddha is especially important for Japanese death practices. Devotion to the Amida Buddha is associated with a good death and rebirth in the Pure Land, a domain believed to be conducive to attaining buddhahood and enlightenment.

Historically, these bone buddhas were a creative innovation that offered a beautiful solution for temples with a difficult problem: what to do with the bones left in their care of those who had nobody to claim their remains, such as the poor, travelers and foreigners.

Today, the few temples that offer this rare practice accept full or partial bones – even just several grams of bones – which are collected and held at the temple until there are sufficient bones to construct a bone buddha.

Others opt for “hakajimai,” or grave-closing, in which the urns buried in a family grave are disinterred and the bones are reinterred elsewhere, such as a communal ossuary. Abandoned and neglected graves are seen as a blight – emblematic of the collapse of the traditional family system of caring for the dead. The process of “hakajimai” ends the family’s responsibility for maintaining the family grave and paying regular dues.
People opt for “hakajimai” because it ends the logistical, financial and emotional costs of maintaining the family grave and does not pass on those burdens to the next generation.
How the living interact with the dead
In Japan, the dead remain part of the social worlds of the living. Family relationships and ritual obligations maintain the connections of the dead and the living across generations.

Traditional rituals are becoming difficult to sustain. Nevertheless, people are still finding ways to remain connected to the dead. Changing burial practices is one way in which people are reshaping old traditions to accommodate modern demands.
