articles.title: Activists push for Pakistan to recognise and support people with albinism
articles.author: Mahpara Zulqadar
paras: Pakistan keeps no data on people with albinism, leaving needs unmet in schools, healthcare, and jobs.
Originally published on Global Voices
Graph from the 2021 study “Genetic Causes of Oculocutaneous Albinism in Pakistani Population.” Sajid et al., Genes 2021, 12(4), 492. CC BY 4.0 via MDPI.

For Adeel Nasir, 24, who has albinism and lives in Kot Radha Kishan, a town in Kasur district, Punjab Province of Pakistan, school meant constant adjustment to challenges that many people around him did not understand.

Because of low vision, he struggled to read what was written on classroom whiteboards. Some teachers seated him closer to the board, improved the lighting, and gave him written notes. But one classroom incident remained painful.
Adeel once asked a teacher what qualifications a fighter pilot needs. He expected encouragement about his ambition. Instead, he received a response focused on his eyesight.
“First of all, you should be able to see clearly with your eyes,” Adeel recalled the teacher saying.
His classmates laughed. Years later, he says people still notice his condition before they recognise his abilities.
“My abilities, my degrees, and my skills were ignored because of my weak eyesight and physical appearance,” he said during an in-person interview with Global Voices.

Adeel’s experience reflects a concern that Malooka-Anne Miti-Drummond, the UN Independent Expert on the enjoyment of human rights by persons with albinism, raised during her June 2026 visit to Pakistan. She said policies, programmes, and data systems overlook people with albinism.

Albinism is a rare, non-contagious, genetically inherited condition caused by reduced or absent production of melanin, the pigment responsible for colour in the skin, hair, and eyes. Reduced melanin can result in visual impairment and increased vulnerability to ultraviolet (UV) radiation because melanin provides natural protection against sun damage. People with albinism are born with the condition; it is not contagious and does not affect their intellectual ability.

Pakistan has no separate national estimate of how many people with albinism live in the country. The UN notes that country-level data on albinism is scarce worldwide, and many countries collect no official statistics on it. Available estimates put prevalence at roughly one in 17,000 to 20,000 people in many European and North American populations, and higher in some African communities. The UN has called for better data collection to understand the challenges people with albinism face.

The absence of a national estimate does not mean that people with albinism are absent in Pakistan. Researchers have documented albinism among Pakistani families despite the missing estimate. A study of 94 previously unreported Pakistani families with non-syndromic oculocutaneous albinism found disease-causing variants mainly in the TYR and OCA2 genes, two of the major genetic causes of albinism worldwide. Genetic studies of affected families cannot establish how many people with albinism live in the country.

For Adeel, the lack of recognition shapes how institutions treat his needs. After a long effort, he obtained a disability certificate, but as he explained, “The disability certificate we received is also issued on the basis of our weak eyesight, not because of albinism itself.”
“There is no place in any office or government institution where a separate form or category under the name of ‘albino’ exists where we can register ourselves,” Adeel added.
When a community is missing from data

The difficulty of documenting albinism ties to a broader gap in disability data. Many national systems measure disability through functional difficulties and do not record each medical condition separately. Pakistan’s 2023 Population and Housing Census asked about difficulty seeing, hearing, walking, communicating, remembering, and caring for oneself rather than individual conditions.

A Pakistan Bureau of Statistics representative, who spoke to Global Voices on condition of anonymity, said the bureau keeps no separate official data on people with albinism. The person said collecting information on rare conditions requires well-designed questionnaires, and Pakistan would have to choose the best method before adding albinism to future data collection.
Asim Zafar, a disability rights advocate, emphasised that data is essential during an interview with Global Voices via WhatsApp:
“Data is very important for any country because planning is done on the basis of data, and budget allocation is done on the basis of planning.”
Miti-Drummond identified that missing data limits access to healthcare, education, and social protection: “When communities are not visible, their needs are not visible.”
Education, healthcare and everyday barriers

Sundus Arif, 39, was born and raised in Lahore, Pakistan. She has albinism and low vision, and she said in an online interview with Global Voices that her biggest challenge has often been getting others to understand her needs.

Her schools had no structured accommodations, so she had to explain her condition and advocate for adjustments herself. As a student, she needed simple measures: a seat in the shade during outdoor assemblies, larger-print material, and extra time to copy notes from the board. She said:
“There are neither clear guidelines nor effective arrangements in educational institutions of Pakistan to accommodate students with albinism.”
Adeel said small adjustments helped him stay in school, but he received no extra time in examinations despite his visual difficulties.
Miti-Drummond said bullying and a lack of support erode the confidence of children with albinism and hurt their education: “If a child is bullied, they are more likely to drop out of school.”

People with albinism also face specific healthcare needs for their skin and vision. Because melanin protects against UV radiation, they are more vulnerable to sun damage and need sun protection and regular medical care. Access to dermatological and eye care is a concern for people with albinism worldwide.
Sundus, also a parent of a child with albinism, said children need sunscreen and sunglasses to protect their skin and eyes from sunlight.
Miti-Drummond explained family income decides whether households can afford that protection:
“If you have to choose between sunscreen and buying food, and you are already struggling to buy food, this is something that becomes inaccessible.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) says early eye care, sun protection, and access to health information can reduce many of the complications linked to albinism. It recognises sunscreen as an important preventive measure because reduced melanin raises vulnerability to UV damage.

Education does not remove social barriers for many people with albinism. Adeel said finding work was one of his biggest challenges after he finished his studies. He believes employers focused on his eyesight and appearance instead of his qualifications.
Miti-Drummond also pointed to employment discrimination worldwide: “You may be very well qualified, but actually getting employment, there was still stigma and discrimination.”

During the interview, Sundus said women with albinism face discrimination beyond disability-related barriers. Social expectations about appearance, marriage, and femininity add pressure. In her experience, people judged her appearance before they noticed her education, professional abilities, or personality. Women with albinism often have to challenge misconceptions about both their condition and their role in society.
Climate change adds another risk

Rising temperatures and frequent heatwaves in Pakistan add to the risk of sun exposure for people with albinism. Pakistan is among the countries most affected by climate change, and national climate assessments document rising temperatures, extreme heat events, and growing climate-related risks.

A study in the BMJ Global Health journal reported that climate change may increase vulnerability among people with albinism by intensifying exposure-related risks and creating barriers to preventive healthcare in low-resource settings.
For Adeel, heat and sunlight shape daily life. Sensitivity to sunlight makes it hard for him to move around outdoors, and he described problems with his skin and eyesight.

Several countries have built specific frameworks for people with albinism. Miti-Drummond told Global Voices that efforts in Malawi, Cameroon, Tanzania, Mozambique, Uganda, Angola, and Panama improved awareness, healthcare access, education and protection from discrimination. For Pakistan, the first step is better information and inclusive planning.
Zafar said laws and policies fall short without implementation:
“Policies are available, laws have been made, but there is a lack of implementation.”
For Adeel, recognition means people with albinism should not have to fight individually for basic support.

Albinism is present across Pakistan, and existing systems do not recognise the needs of the people who live with it. Better data would make them visible. Inclusion also takes accessible healthcare, inclusive education, climate-sensitive planning and a voice for people with albinism in decisions that affect their lives. Miti-Drummond put the principle in four words: “Nothing for us without us.”
For Pakistan’s people with albinism, being counted is the first step, but being heard and included is the ultimate goal.

articles.title: Video game film adaptations used to be huge flops. Now studios can’t get enough
articles.author: Liam Burke, Associate Professor and Cinema and Screen Studies Discipline Leader, Swinburne University of Technology
paras: In the early 1990s, when the home video game market was still in its infancy, Hollywood attempted to leverage the appeal of this emerging entertainment for feature length films.
The resulting movies – including Super Mario Bros. (1993), Mortal Kombat (1995), and the Jean Claude Van Damme-starring Street Fighter (1994) – largely bombed in their critical reception.

Today, however, video game to film adaptations are filling multiplexes, from blockbusters such as A Minecraft Movie (2025), to elevated horrors such as the recent Resident Evil (2026) film, and lower-budget breakouts like Iron Lung (2026).
As Street Fighter swing-kicks its way back into cinemas, it’s worth looking at how, and why, the video game-to-film pipeline has started gushing anew.
Film studios favour projects that will simultaneously appeal to younger and older audiences. This explains why there are so many live action Disney remakes.
The current video game film adaptation trend kicked off around 2020 – made possible by a cross-generational audience that didn’t exist a few decades ago.

The 1994 Street Fighter film was distributed in US cinemas just a few years after the first game arrived on home consoles. The latest adaptation, on the other hand, will appeal to generations of fans familiar with characters like Ryu, Ken and Chun-Li.
Media commentator Patrick Metzger’s concept of the “nostalgia pendulum” describes how pop culture regularly revives trends from about 30 years earlier.
The new Street Fighter film leans heavily into 90s nostalgia. Set in 1993, it invoked touchstones such as Jolt Cola, MTV, and era-defining music like Tupac Shakur’s track Ambitionz Az a Ridah.
The fact these video game have stood the test of time has also earned them cultural legitimacy.

In the early 90s, video games were treated as a comparative novelty. When they were considered at all by tastemakers, it was usually in panicked terms about their addictive qualities or violent content.
But today’s audiences – who are also today’s filmmakers and critics – have grown up playing video games.

Promoting Street Fighter, director Kitao Sakurai emphasised his personal longstanding connection to the games. Critics, too, have compared the film seriously with its source material, rather than dismissing it as dumb, loud and violent.

Transmedia storyworlds such as the Marvel Cinematic Universe and the Wizarding World of Harry Potter are big business. They don’t just allow one story to be told; they provide multiple film sequels, TV spin-offs, theme park attractions, merchandise lines and even Broadway shows.
Video game universes are similarly ripe for creative mining, especially those that have been expanding since the 90s.

It’s telling that the phenomenally popular sandbox game Minecraft was adapted not as The Minecraft Movie, but “A Minecraft Movie”: the indefinite article indicates it is just one of many stories within its world. (And yes, a sequel is confirmed).
A Mario that actually looks like Mario
Video game adaptations have also been hugely bolstered by advances in digital technologies.
In the early 90s, blockbuster films still used practical effects, while video games relied on two-dimensional sprites. This created a technological gulf that made convincing adaptations difficult.

Moving into the 21st century, Hollywood’s growing embrace of digital production – and the shift towards 3D gaming (accelerated by consoles such as PlayStation) – narrowed the visual gap between the two media.

Writing about The Matrix franchise in 2006, media scholar Henry Jenkins observed how: “the game world can now look almost exactly like the film world – because they are reusing many of the same digital assets”.

Video games can now be adapted with a degree of visual fidelity that was impossible in earlier eras – even allowing Jason Momoa to transform into the green-skinned monster Blanka in the new Street Fighter.

Media conglomerates such as Disney, Universal and the Skydance Corporation (which oversees the recently merged studios Warner Bros. and Paramount), recognise video game worlds as a valuable foundation for transmedia franchises.

Many of these conglomerates are integrating games into their corporate strategies. In 2024, Disney acquired a 9% stake in Fortnite publisher Epic Games. The companies announced plans for a shared “social universe” that will extend Disney properties such as Marvel and Star Wars into new gaming experiences.
Video game companies also view adaptation as a way to cross-promote their properties and expand audiences.
Zach Cregger’s recent Resident Evil film was the eighth film adaptation in the horror franchise, but the first to involve Sony’s PlayStation Productions.
Executive producer Oliver Berben said the partnership created opportunities for both PlayStation and parent company Sony to promote the wider franchise across their platforms.
PlayStation Productions is a Sony subsidiary that was founded in 2019 to adapt popular PlayStation games into films, such as Uncharted (2022), Gran Turismo (2023) and Until Dawn (2025).

Like arcade gamers lining up their coins for the next turn, Hollywood studios have dozens of video game films currently in production. The Legend of Zelda, Elden Ring and Call of Duty are all due for their own films within the next two years.
Clearly, the video game adaptation trend won’t be ending anytime soon.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: At the UN, plans for a global coalition to attack LGBTQ+ and reproductive rights
articles.author: Uncloseted Media
paras: Far-right activists are trying to dismantle global protections for LGBTQ+ people under the guise of ‘family values’
Originally published on Global Voices
US President Trump speaking at the U.N. General Assembly. Photo by The White House. Fair use.

This article by Hope Pisoni was originally published by Uncloseted Media, an LGBTQ+ focused investigative news outlet, on October 1, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices as part of a content partnership agreement. It has been edited for length and style.

On September 17, while the United Nations (U.N.) was hosting its annual General Assembly for diplomats and leaders from all over the world, several key figures filled a room across the street at the Millennium Hilton in Midtown Manhattan. Attendees included Trump administration officials, leaders of anti-LGBTQ+ hate groups, far-right politicians from Latin America and reporters from far-right media.

These people were meeting for the Global Forum for Life, Family and Freedoms, a two-day summit of right-wing leaders with an ambitious goal to create a new “pro-life and pro-family” Core Group at the U.N.

Since 2008, the U.N. has had an LGBTI Core Group with 42 member states whose mission is to advocate for LGBTQ+ rights on a global stage. But the organizers of this new group hope to create an opposing organization to push for policies that undermine reproductive and LGBTQ+ rights around the globe.

Aarón Lara, the Mexico-based conservative activist who came up with the idea for the group, said in an August article that the existing LGBTI Core Group has only been successful because there has not been organized conservative opposition, which a new core group would provide.
Lara (left) speaking with a reporter in the Dominican Republic in March. Screenshot via Central Noticias YouTube.

“[The LGBTI Core Group] has successfully established victimhood narratives and incorporated observances with global impact. … I always use this example: If it were a soccer match and one team failed to show up, the winner by default would be the team that was present,” Lara said.

Lara and other supporters of the group agreed at the forum to draw up plans for its creation in the coming months. They may be encouraged to move quickly because the group’s leaders have said they want to use the U.S.’s global influence and capitalize on the current administration’s anti-LGBTQ and anti-abortion stance to do it. The U.S. recently left the LGBTI Core Group, an early move by Trump in his second term.

The LGBTI Core Group describes itself as “an informal cross-regional group of United Nations Member States.” While it is not an official U.N. body, its work includes ensuring that LGBTQ+ people are considered and protected across all of the U.N.’s activities, from humanitarian aid to human rights resolutions.

For example, one of the first U.N. resolutions to reference LGBTQ+ people was one protecting civilians against extrajudicial executions. When some members tried to remove LGBTQ people from those protections, advocates and allies fought to keep them in place. Maria Sjödin, executive director of Outright International, an NGO that focuses on supporting LGBTQ rights worldwide, told Uncloseted Media that work like this could be in jeopardy should the new core group come to fruition.

“We’re talking about the protection of some very basic human rights, and that the opposition to that is trying to organize to make it even more difficult to pass such a thing is really quite horrible,” she says.

Core groups are not official U.N. bodies, so there is no strictly required procedure for their creation. While there have been other core groups established at the U.N., the LGBTI group is unique in that it is designed for continuous operation on multiple issues rather than as a response to a specific conflict or crisis. The “pro-life, pro-family” core group would change that, threatening to shift the balance of power at the U.N.

Ipas, an international NGO that seeks to increase access to safe abortions and contraception, shared a briefing paper, “The Pro-Life and Pro-Family Core Group: The Evangelical Architecture Supporting Anti-Gender Initiatives at the United Nations,” with Uncloseted Media. It explains that this core group would allow anti-LGBTQ+ and anti-abortion governments to collaborate on “coordinated voting” to “dilute, block, or impose conditions on language regarding sexual and reproductive health and rights.” The briefing also predicts that the core group would accelerate existing efforts to portray anti-LGBTQ+ politics as “sovereign resistance” against “globalism” in the public eye.

“This discourse … asserts national sovereignty over agreed-upon international human rights, reframing sexual and reproductive rights as an external imposition rather than as already recognized human rights standards,” the briefing reads.

Lara is the founder and president of the Ibero-American Congress for Life and Family (CIVF). Founded in Mexico City in 2017, CIVF describes itself as “Un movimiento de reforma moral, educativa, social y jurídica por la vida y la familia” (a movement for moral, educational, social, and legal reform for life and family) and is best known for holding an annual congress for leaders, primarily from Latin America and Spain, to discuss the promotion of socially conservative policies.
In a 2021 article in an evangelical publication, Lara said that his group had applied to become a core group at the U.N.
“We have the conviction that it is our responsibility as believers to be a light in the midst of darkness, this is why [we] are making this big effort,” he said.
The third CIVF, held in Panama in 2019. Image from CIVF via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.

While that application never came to fruition, Lara remained interested in starting a U.N. core group, and announced in July 2026 that CIVF — which did not respond to Uncloseted Media’s request for comment — was launching a new plan to do so.
How did the US get involved?

The following month, Lara shared more details of the plan with The Washington Stand, a news outlet owned by Family Research Council, a Southern Poverty Law Center-designated anti-LGBTQ hate group closely affiliated with Focus on the Family. In the article, Lara says the goal is for the U.S. to sponsor the new group because of its powerful position on the world stage.

Sjödin is concerned about U.S. involvement in a group like this. “[It] already has an outsized influence on the world, so the U.S. potentially taking on a leadership role in a coalition like this also risks the effects being outsized and makes this an initiative that is going to be more difficult to challenge,” she says.
Valerie Huber speaking at CPAC Hungary in 2022. Image by Elekes Andor via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.

To that end, CIVF enlisted Valerie Huber, an influential American ally based in Washington, D.C., in their fight. Huber, who co-led the September 17th forum alongside Lara, is an American right-wing activist who held multiple leadership roles at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) during Trump’s first term. She has consistently promoted the exclusion of LGBTQ+ people in her work — the organization she led before getting her HHS appointment released a guideline that said “it would be inappropriate and unethical to assert or affirm” trans kids’ genders.

“Valerie Huber is internationally recognized in the anti-rights space,” Wendy Via, co-founder and president of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, told Uncloseted Media. “She is bringing some credibility [and] influence to the idea of creating a separate core group, so she’s gonna be able to get people to join with her.”

During her tenure at HHS, Huber helped craft the Geneva Consensus Declaration on Promoting Women’s Health and Strengthening the Family (GCD), an agreement between 46 countries, including the U.S. under both Trump administrations, affirming a commitment to hardline opposition to abortion and promoting the heteronormative nuclear family “as foundational to society.”

Critics have noted that many of the agreement’s signatories are led by notoriously authoritarian governments with harsh restrictions on LGBTQ+ people. For example, Saudi Arabia’s maximum penalty for gay sex is death, and Russia classifies the “international LGBT movement” as an extremist group.

During his first week in office, former president Joe Biden withdrew the U.S. from the GCD just months after its launch, stating, “It is the policy of my Administration to support women’s and girls’ sexual and reproductive health and rights in the United States, as well as globally.”

But Huber, now out of her government job and leading the anti-abortion NGO Institute for Women’s Health (IWH), continued to champion the agreement. She’s traveled around the world meeting heads of state, including in Burundi and Argentina, who would quickly go on to join the GCD, while developing more concrete plans to carry out its goals. IWH did not respond to a request for comment.

Within the first week of Trump’s second term, the U.S. rejoined the agreement, and in June, the U.S. assumed the leading secretariat position among its signatories. Via says pushing the core group initiative while the U.S. is the secretariat is likely strategic timing.

“The U.N. is seen as the boogeyman for far-right and Christian Nationalist groups, because their definition of human rights is expansive and inclusive, which is not what these organizations want,” Via says. “But they’re gonna work within the system because it looks like they have an opportunity.”
Huber has advocated in favor of the core group since August and has said that the GCD is “the substantive basis” for the work ahead.

“What has not yet been built is the intentional, sustained coordination that turns a shared commitment into shared strategy at the international negotiating table,” she told The Washington Stand. “A nation that arrives at a negotiation alone is outmatched. A nation that arrives having strategized with 40 others is not.”
The who’s who of the far right are on board
Faith leaders praying over Donald Trump in March 2025. Image via The White House. Fair use.

The September 17th forum was held in the hopes of creating a roadmap to execute the plans for the core group. The event was sponsored by Well Versed, an evangelical NGO whose mission is to bring “biblical principles of governance to government leaders and the people who elect them.”

The forum attracted a number of noteworthy guests. There were three representatives from the Trump administration, including Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, Director of HHS Global Affairs Bethany Kozma, and Ellie Cohanim, the senior policy advisor at the U.S. mission to the U.N.

Leaders from several U.S.-based right-wing organizations also made appearances, including Turning Point USA Faith, C-Fam — which holds special consultative status at the U.N. — and Salt and Light Council, a group focused on getting churches involved in right-wing politics.
Via called these groups “the usual suspects” when it comes to work like this, but noted that their power has grown in recent years.

In addition to the power players from the U.S., there was a stacked lineup of folks from the global right. Lawmakers from Peru, Uruguay, and Guatemala, all countries where CIVF has been active, were present. Also in attendance was Artur Pawlowski, a Canadian far-right pastor known for his role in the Alberta Separatist movement; Armenian evangelical activist and former politician Stepan Sargsyan; and Dutch lobbyist Henk Jan van Schothorst.
What this lineup indicates, Via says, is that the Christian far-right is interested in wielding its outsized influence in the Trump administration to impact the global stage.

“It is the traction that the Christian nationalists have gained since Trump has been in office,” she says. “Because of the administration’s willingness to wield power and influence in other countries based on this Biblical worldview … you have had some political leaders be more accepting of the idea.”

In her interview for The Washington Stand, Huber said that the point of the core group is to organize concrete action towards the goals of the GCD, which on its own is a non-binding agreement with no mechanism to enforce or ensure compliance among its signatories.

One way the core group should achieve that, Huber says, is through Protego, a project launched in 2023 by IWH that creates a road map for countries to follow in their policymaking on issues of women’s health. Outlined in their Women’s Optimal Health Framework, IWH advocates against abortion and promotes sex education that prioritizes abstinence and “prepar[ing] for a healthy marriage and future family.”

While the 62-page guide makes no explicit mention of LGBTQ people, Sjödin says that this kind of sex education, which has been widely criticized as ineffective, “is focused on promoting heterosexuality as the only form of acceptable sexuality.”

“It is used to push these binary norms that are harmful for anyone who doesn’t live up to it or doesn’t agree with it, and it limits access to education for young people who need to know both about themselves, especially if they don’t think of themselves as heterosexual, but also about everyone else so that they have an understanding that humans are different.”
Giammattei speaking at an IWH conference in 2021. Screenshot via the Government of Guatemala YouTube.

A few countries have already adopted Protego’s framework. Guatemala was the first, establishing a partnership with Huber and the IWH in June 2023 under the leadership of far-right then-president Alejandro Giammattei. The Protego project worked with the country’s Ministries of Health, Education and Social Development and developed a “Parent Child Communication Guide” that would promote IWH’s narratives on sex and family planning to Guatemalans.
Huber claims the guide, which was spread throughout the country via partnerships with influencers and faith and business leaders, has reached 3 million school-aged children in Guatemala.
Huber and Ugandan First Lady Janet Museveni signing the agreement of their partnership on Protego in 2024. Screenshot via UBC Television Uganda YouTube.

Uganda, where gay sex is punishable by death, was the next country to adopt the framework in early 2024. Unlike in Guatemala, specific details have been difficult to access and not publicly shared, but promoting abstinence-only sex education has been a publicly stated priority.
Other countries, including Hungary and Burundi, have also signaled their support for Protego, but less is known about their actions on the matter.
While the new core group has not yet been officially established, statements by Lara and Huber suggest an intention to do so in the near future.

“[It will take] less time than people assume, because the hardest part is already done,” Huber said in her Washington Stand interview. “The coalition exists. The shared commitments are on paper and have held through changes of government in multiple countries.”
Ipas, in its briefing, emphasizes that there is still a way to go before the core group’s establishment and cautions advocates to “avoid overstating [its] legitimacy and power.”
However, Sjödin warns that the plans, and the danger they present, must be taken seriously.

“Currently, we are seeing quite an extensive and horrendous backlash against LGBTQ+ people,” she says. “What they potentially want to do here is to actually make inclusion of everyone more difficult.”
